title: Kshama, forbearance
hookLine: the Gita lists forgiveness among the divine qualities (Bhagavad Gita 16.3)

cards: A word turns up in a list, an odd place to meet something so hard to do.
In the sixteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna about two kinds of nature a person can be born to, one he calls divine and one demonic.
He names the divine qualities first, one after another, like things packed for a long journey. Fearlessness. Purity of heart.

teach.b: Look at its neighbors. In the same verse, right beside kshama, are vigor and fortitude, the strength to keep going under pressure. A little earlier comes freedom from anger.
Forgiveness here keeps strong company. It isn't among the soft extras; it's packed in with the steel.

Kshama is translated forgiveness, and also forbearance or patience: the capacity to bear what's done to you without striking back. Less a single act after a fight, more a settled way of holding wrongs as they come.
Krishna says this on a battlefield, to a man about to go to war. So the Gita isn't describing someone with no enemies, sitting somewhere peaceful.

It's describing a person who may have to act, even firmly, and still carries forbearance inside. Hindu teachers read that tension in different ways, and the Gita leaves room for them. Last, whose quality it is.

teach.h: A MARK OF THE ONE WHO FORGIVES.
teach.b: Kshama is listed as a mark of the one who forgives. Nothing in the verse makes it wait on the other person's apology, or on their deserving it.
It's part of a divine nature, and some teachers read the list as something a person can grow into. That turns the usual question around. Not, have they earned my forgiveness?
But, what kind of nature am I growing?

how: Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita's list of divine qualities in chapter 16 as a picture of the character to grow toward, and kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is taught as one of them.

o: forbearance: bearing a wrong without striking back
a vow of silence kept during a fast
a calm that comes only after long meditation

s: in the Gita, kshama is listed among the divine qualities
it comes near the end of the list, in chapter 16, verse 3.
Krishna teaches this list in a quiet forest retreat
he says it on a battlefield, to Arjuna before a war.
kshama only counts once the other person has apologized
it's listed as a mark of the one who forgives, not a reward for the one forgiven.

games.q: you're reading Krishna's list of divine qualities. which words sit right beside kshama in Gita 16.3?
games.why: vigor and fortitude. forgiveness keeps strong company in the Gita's list.

practice: Picture a moment later today when someone is likely to irritate you, a driver, a coworker, a slow line, and feel the small heat that comes with it.

Now picture bearing it: not pretending it's fine, just letting it arrive and pass through without striking back, breathing out slowly as if making room. If you pray, you can ask for kshama in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Kshama. Sanskrit for forgiveness and forbearance, listed among the divine qualities in the Bhagavad Gita, beside vigor and fortitude. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: packed in with the steel. Forbearance takes strength, not softness. Day nine hundred sixty-one, done.
